t: Why Service Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy gement-strategy/
q: Encouraging your students to become service-oriented is a powerful classroom management strategy.
It causes them to see their classmates as people just like them, with the same hopes, feelings, and struggles.
Service is an active form of helpfulness. Meaning, you don’t wait until someone asks. It’s something you look for and act upon, even when it’s inconvenient.
Your students are more influenced by what you do than what you say.
As for finding the time for it, with good classroom management comes the freedom not to have to rush through anything . It buys you oceans of time few other teachers enjoy.
Make your classroom more than just the acquisition of knowledge. Develop the whole person by being a classroom defined by service.
x: He notes today's students tend to embrace service readily, and that good classroom management creates the surplus time needed to fit it in, with most administrators supportive when given advance notice.

t: 6 Teaching Insights I Gained through Writing a Book
q: As a teacher, I want the courses I teach to be 1% of the reason that my students go on to lead flourishing lives.
So you can't know if you're making something powerful while you're making it, but there are still things you can do.
It's possible to be an okay teacher by just showing up and doing a few things well. And in a sense, I want more of us to be okay with being okay.
After all, neomania is making us crazier (and less effective) teachers. New only makes sense when we clearly understand why what we already have isn't working.
Great teachers don't magically come into work with this other-oriented bent — they cultivate it, day by day, through earnest, internal work.
I need to have something, a sense of the whole of teaching, that's simple enough to hold in my head but robust enough to explore for a lifetime.
Year by year, I've moved from the guy who quit to the guy who sees himself doing this for his whole career.

q: To help ensure you begin the school year on the right classroom management foot, I compiled a list of questions.
I recommend initially running through the questions quickly, answering with your gut instinct.
Am I 100% committed to following my classroom management plan as it’s written?
Every year I get a flurry of emails and coaching sign-ups beginning the third week of school from teachers desperate to know how to rein in an out of control class .
It’s definitely possible, even if their class is in open rebellion. But it’s a far greater challenge than getting it right the first time.
Because once you can answer yes to all fourteen questions, you’re ready to mold your new group of students into the dream class you really want.

t: How To Increase Maturity And Independence Tenfold
q: Right or wrong, today’s students have less freedom than in decades past. Generally speaking, their lives are more controlled, organized, and edited.

All the guiding, advising, directing, and micromanaging very effectively weakens our students’ internal self-starter mechanism. It paralyzes their imagination, creativity, and ability to visualize, set, and attain their own goals.

It is this: Whenever your students are doing what you want, asked of them, or expected—no matter what it is— leave them alone . As much as possible, you want to disappear, become a fly on the wall, and just observe .

The moment they begin giving you what you want, don’t step in to praise or encourage. Don’t narrate, remind, or rehash. Don’t kneel down and ask questions or offer hints and clues. Don’t even acknowledge.

The idea is for them to forget that you’re even there, to rely on themselves and their classmates, and to carry the full weight of responsibility—which feels good and empowers them with the ability to know how to learn and succeed no matter the obstacles.
This is what is expected.” “You can do this.” “You don’t need me.” “I believe in you.
x: Today's students are said to have less unstructured freedom than past generations, contributing to rising immaturity and dependency.

The core strategy: once students are doing what's expected, the teacher should disappear entirely—no praise, narrating, reminders, or acknowledgment.

t: The Business and Educational Sense of Selfless Service
q: It seems that the best online businesspeople have a good deal in common with the best teachers, at least in three ways.
When we humble ourselves to the “never finished” nature of teaching, it makes us better and more believable.
Experience has taught these people — like it teaches us teachers — that failure is normal, and it can even be generative for future success.
when you aim at the highest good for your audience — the best book for them, the best course, the most transformative teaching — you can get pretty great lower-level results thrown in, too.
In teaching, when we aim at the highest good of our students — their long-term flourishing by way of mastering our course material — we get the rest thrown in.
It's just that the test gets a seat in the back of the airplane — it doesn't get to be the pilot.
It can't be lip service — none of this, “We want what's best for kids” when we really just want them to score high on the state test.

t: How To Have Better, Sharper Routines Next School Year
q: Routines are the lifeblood of a well-run classroom. Because, done right, they save tons of learning time.
Her routines felt laborious. Her students would perform them, but reluctantly and often poorly. Every transition was becoming a downer and a drain on her patience.
The answer is a simple little thing, but it can be a very big deal: She was (and her students were) doing them too slow .
For routines to be most effective, for them to be sharp and efficient and for students to be motivated to perform them, they should be done as fast as possible without becoming sloppy .
It works because speeding them up adds an element of challenge, which is not only fulfilling and enjoyable for students, but it will change their perspective and attitude toward performing them.
So this coming school year, try performing your routines just 10% faster. Make em’ snappy.
x: The concrete recommendation is to try performing classroom routines about 10% faster in the coming school year.
Routines should be executed as fast as possible without becoming sloppy; excessive slowness drains energy and invites complaint.
